name: Priya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Ashgrove Dairy, 320 cows. We've got four milking robots, so the cows walk in and get milked when they want, day or night. My day starts at six with the phone, actually. The system flags which cows haven't been milked, who's eating less, who might be coming into heat. Then I walk the shed and check what the screen told me against what I see. I love that bit, when the data and my eyes agree. What wears me out is the 3 a.m. alarms when a robot jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I've got an assistant that reads the herd reports and tells me which twelve cows to look at first. I use it to plan the feed ration too, then check with our nutritionist. My partner Sam works in IT for the water company, so we talk tech over dinner, probably too much. We rent a house in Ashgrove village and have about five months saved. The owners, the Bells, are good to work for, but it's their farm, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, well. That's sort of where we already are, isn't it? A bit of help, no revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the tools are useful, use them, but stop pretending they're magic. And I'd say the real gain should go to the workers, because when I save the Bells two hours a day, I don't see any of that in my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I like this stuff. I'd hoped it would let me spot lameness a week early, or get the ration right to the gram. In this picture it stays a clever helper, not a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep pushing the tools as far as they go. I'd probably start a small side business helping other dairies set up their herd software, since three farmers have already asked me. And I'd keep five months saved, maybe grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. Like I'd been promised a new tractor and got a new seat cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gain should go to workers. Have you asked the Bells for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring. I showed them the robot data saved them a part-time wage. They gave me a bonus, which was nice, but it was a one-off. I'd want it in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the farmers who asked you for help.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Tom at Hollow Lane, Mrs Okafor's place, and the young couple who took over Ridge Farm. They've all got robots and no idea how to read the reports. I could charge for a Saturday each and it would pay my car insurance.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are useful but nobody should pretend they're magic. I'd also say the time AI saves should show up in workers' pay, not just the owners' profits.
S0.think: Privately she'd feel let down, because she hoped AI would spot lameness early and get rations exact. In this picture it stays a clever helper, not a real partner.
S0.do: Keeps pushing the herd tools as far as they'll go and starts weekend paid help for three nearby dairies with their software. Holds and grows her five months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm but restless, like being promised a new tractor and getting a seat cover.
S0.quote: Like I'd been promised a new tractor and got a new seat cover.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is the rare farmer who'd be disappointed if AI stalled. Her left-leaning view shows up as a concrete pay demand: share the time savings with staff. She already has a ready-made side business waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, now we're talking. This one excites me and worries me about equally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if we do it right. Farms can be kinder to animals and to people with this stuff. But I'd also say, and I'd post it, that the workers have to get a share, through the union or through profit-sharing, or it'll just make the owners richer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'm the person on the farm who understands the systems. The ones I'd worry about are Lukas, our relief milker, and Mandy who does the calves. Their jobs are the ones the machines take next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd put together a proper proposal for the Bells: more automation in the calf shed, and I'd train Mandy on the monitoring side so she moves up, not out. I'd grow the side business to five or six farms. I'd ask for a profit share in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. Like the first day of harvest when you know it's going to be long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be pushing automation that takes Mandy's job. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I just did it to cut costs. That's why I'd tie it to training her. If the Bells won't pay for that, I'd still say it, loudly. I'm not going to be the person who automates my friend out of a job and calls it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say go for it, and then ask if the profit share is in writing. He's more careful with contracts than me. Which is useful.

S1.say: I'd say this is good if done right, because farms can be kinder to animals and people. I'd post that workers must get a share through the union or profit-sharing.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she'd be fine as the person who understands the systems. She worries for the relief milker and the calf worker, whose jobs come next.
S1.do: Proposes more automation in the calf shed tied to training her colleague Mandy for a monitoring role. Grows her advice business to five or six farms and asks for a written profit share.
S1.feel: Uneasy but energised, like the first day of a long harvest.
S1.quote: I'm not going to be the person who automates my friend out of a job and calls it progress.
S1.fieldNote: She's both the driver of automation and its conscience on the farm. Her answer to the tension is to tie every new machine to training a colleague. She's confident about her own place in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... the robots I use now, but smarter than me. Hm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this needs public ownership or at least huge taxes on the AI companies, because otherwise a few firms own all the work. I'd be loud on it online, which I don't normally bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first picture where I lose. My edge is that I understand the systems better than the owners do. If the system understands itself, I'm just a person who used to be clever. That's hard to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd move my side business from setting up software to helping farms through the change, because they'd all be panicking. I'd save hard, aim for nine months. When it arrived, I'd join the union's campaign properly and look at jobs where a person signs off on what the AI decides, like animal welfare inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit dizzy. I'm used to being ahead, and here I'd just be early to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change for someone who adapts quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means being quick doesn't help much. Normally I win by getting there first. Two years is too short to build anything new that a machine won't also do by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mandy and Lukas the week it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not about who's good with computers anymore, we're all in it. I'd ask them both to come to the union meeting with me. I'd probably apologise to Mandy for the calf shed plan.

S2.say: I'd say this needs public ownership or heavy taxes on AI companies, or a few firms will own all the work. I'd be loud about it online, which isn't like her.
S2.think: Privately she sees it as the first picture where she loses, because her edge is understanding the systems. If the systems understand themselves, she's just someone who used to be clever.
S2.do: Turns her side business toward helping farms through the change and saves hard toward nine months. Joins the union campaign and looks at roles where people sign off on AI decisions, such as animal welfare inspection.
S2.feel: Anxious and a bit dizzy, because being early would only mean losing first.
S2.quote: If the system understands itself, I'm just a person who used to be clever.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips her advantage: speed of learning stops mattering. Her politics sharpen toward public ownership. She shows real feeling for colleagues, including an apology she hasn't been asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. I'd be thirty-two. That's a whole second go at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to set the rules, while there's a window. I'd push for a law that says farms that automate pay into a training fund for their staff. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd start retraining tomorrow. Not in coding. In animal welfare and food safety law, because someone will have to decide what the machines are allowed to do to animals. I think that's a person's job for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start an evening course in animal welfare science, about two thousand a year from savings. I'd keep the herd job and the side business going. By year three I'd apply to the government inspection service. I'd use AI every day to study, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. There's a path I can see from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're sure people will still make those calls. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm wrong, and I'll be in the same place as everyone else. But I'd rather bet on the job that's about deciding what's right than the job that's about doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course without draining the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The side business. Six farms at a Saturday a month covers it. Sam says I should keep the five months untouched and he's right.

S3.say: I'd say this is the window to set rules, like a law making automating farms pay into a training fund for staff. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone listening.
S3.think: Privately she'd start retraining at once in animal welfare and food safety, not coding. She thinks deciding what machines may do to animals will stay a human job.
S3.do: Starts an evening animal welfare science course at about two thousand a year, paid from her side business, while keeping the herd job. Aims to apply to the government inspection service by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, because she can see a path from here.
S3.quote: I'd rather bet on the job that's about deciding what's right than the job that's about doing the work.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she makes a clear bet on judgement over skill. Her plan is unusually precise on money and timing. She admits honestly she could be wrong about which jobs stay human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd probably change my mind three times about what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, and if we use it, this could be the best thing that ever happened to farm animals and farm workers. Shorter weeks, no 3 a.m. alarms. But only if the gains are shared, which I'd keep banging on about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Ten years is enough for me to become one of the people who runs the systems for a whole region, or inspects them. The risk for me is getting comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First three years, I'd grow the side business into a proper small company, maybe with one employee. I'd do the welfare course part-time. Somewhere around year five, I'd talk to Sam about whether we buy a house or keep renting, because I'd want to know what my work looks like first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, actually. With a small knot of 'don't get smug'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a house. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage ties you to a place, and in this picture I don't know where the work will be. Maybe the job's in the city, at a regional control centre. I'd rather stay light for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd lose my edge before I could use it. Ten years, my edge is worth something. For someone like me, time is everything. For Mandy, I'm not sure time helps as much.

S4.say: I'd say with a decade, this could be the best thing for farm animals and workers, with shorter weeks and no 3 a.m. alarms. But only if the gains are shared.
S4.think: Privately she thinks she'd do well, running or inspecting systems for a whole region. Her real risk is getting comfortable.
S4.do: Grows her side business into a small company with possibly one employee and keeps studying welfare part-time. Holds off buying a house until around year five, when she knows where the work will be.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and actually excited, with a small knot of worry about getting smug.
S4.quote: For someone like me, time is everything. For Mandy, I'm not sure time helps as much.
S4.fieldNote: Priya is one of the few who'd call the slow AGI picture good news. She notices that time helps people like her more than her less tech-minded colleagues. Housing is her main family decision, and she delays it on purpose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where being good at this stuff doesn't save me. What would help is a law making AI companies and farms that automate pay into a training fund, so people like Mandy get paid time to learn, and a share of the profit for the workers who stay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. In every picture they're the ones who can't say anything. I'd want someone whose job it is to stand up for them, and I'd like it to be me.

headlineQuote: If the system understands itself, I'm just a person who used to be clever.
portrait: Priya Santos is a 27-year-old herd manager at a 320-cow dairy that already milks with robots, and she uses AI tools every day to read herd data and plan feed. She lives with her partner Sam, who works in IT, rents in the village and has about five months saved. She leans left and wants the gains of automation shared through profit-sharing, unions and training funds. She moves first in every picture, but AGI by 2028 is the one where her speed stops helping. With five or ten years she bets on animal welfare inspection, a job about judgement rather than labour.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it's the only picture where being quick and good with technology doesn't protect her.
whatWouldHelp: A law making AI companies and automating farms pay into a training fund so colleagues get paid time to learn, plus a profit share for workers who stay.
